analysis.one_liner: Establishes minimum standards of fair conduct in franchise business relationships.
analysis.headline: The bill received no votes and no cosponsors; it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in March 1993 and died there when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set federal ground rules for the relationship between franchise companies and the people who buy and operate their franchises — fast-food outlets, gas stations, dealerships, and other small businesses. It would have barred franchisors from deceiving prospective buyers, from cutting off a franchisee's franchise without good cause and a chance to fix the problem, from forcing franchisees to buy supplies only from the franchisor, from punishing franchisees for joining together in associations, and from opening new company outlets so close to an existing franchise that they cut its sales. It also imposed duties of good faith and care on franchisors and gave franchisees the right to sue for damages and attorney's fees.
analysis.who_benefits: The bill's direct beneficiaries would have been franchisees — the individuals and families who put their savings into operating a branded business under a franchisor's name and rules. The bill's own findings describe a 'profound imbalance of contractual power' in favor of franchisors and say franchisees often lack 'viable legal recourse' against them. Consumers would benefit indirectly, because the bill states that fairer franchise relationships would produce 'greater benefits' for consumers, and franchisees with healthier businesses tend to compete harder and stay open.

how_it_helps.text: It would prohibit franchisors from committing fraud or deception in selling, operating, or terminating a franchise, and from discriminating among franchisees by race, sex, religion, disability, or national origin.

It would bar a franchisor from terminating a franchise before its term ends without good cause, and would define good cause to require notice and a 30-day period for the franchisee to cure the default.
It would let franchisees buy equipment, fixtures, and supplies from sources of their own choosing, subject to uniform quality standards, rather than being locked into their franchisor's suppliers.
It would protect the right of franchisees to form and join trade associations without retaliation, a power their franchisors could otherwise suppress.

It would restrict franchisors from opening new outlets so close to an existing franchise that the older business loses more than 10 percent of its sales, and would require compensation for losses beyond that.

It would impose duties of good faith and due care on franchisors, a fiduciary duty over pooled advertising funds and bookkeeping services, and give injured franchisees a private right to sue for damages and attorney's fees.

analysis.who_pays: Franchisors — the large companies that sell and control franchises — would bear the cost. They could no longer terminate franchisees freely, could not lock franchisees into buying supplies from them or their affiliates, could not freely open competing company-owned outlets next to franchisees, would face enforceable duties of care and good faith, and would face lawsuits from franchisees with attorney's fees available. Some compliance and litigation costs could ultimately be passed on through the price of goods and services.

drawbacks.text: The bill would restrict standard franchise practices that franchisors defend as necessary to protect brand quality and system consistency — including exclusive supply requirements and the ability to enforce non-compete and non-association terms.

The encroachment rules would make it harder and more costly for franchise companies to expand where they operate, since opening a new outlet near an existing franchise could trigger compensation payments or a requirement to relocate or close the new outlet.
Creating a broad private right of action with attorney's fees could increase litigation between franchisees and franchisors, a cost that could reach consumers through higher prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a genuine imbalance: franchisees invest their own savings but operate under pervasive contractual rights reserved to the franchisor, and the bill's findings say common-law protections had not caught up. The counterweight is real too — franchise systems depend on uniformity, and rules against termination without good cause, mandatory supplier requirements, and encroachment would constrain how franchisors manage quality and growth, with some costs passed through to consumers. On balance, the bill's protections were directed at people who had risked their own assets inside a system they did not control.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never came back out — no hearing, no vote, no cosponsors — until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John LaFalce introduced the bill on March 11, 1993, and it was referred to the House Committee on Judiciary.
On March 18, 1993, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law.
The bill drew no cosponsors and no further action was ever recorded before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Franchisor companies are better off, because a federal floor of fair-dealing rules for franchise relationships never became law and they continue to operate under whatever terms their contracts impose. Franchisees gained nothing from the bill's death; they remain subject to the contract terms their franchisors set.

for.name: Rep. John J. LaFalce
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: House Committee on Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out; it went to the Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law and stayed there for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: International Franchise Association
against.what_they_did: The franchising industry has historically opposed federal legislation regulating franchise relationship practices such as termination and encroachment; no opposition by this group appears in the record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no recorded votes, so its partisan shape was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped franchisors of unilateral termination rights, forced-supplier arrangements, and unrestricted encroachment on their own franchisees, and exposed them to private lawsuits with attorney's fees. Their gain from the bill's death is franchisees' continued exposure to those practices.

Franchisees would have gained contractual protections, collective-association rights, and a private right of action; because the bill died, they remain in the position the bill described as lacking viable legal recourse.
